analysis.one_liner: Bans very large mergers outright and lets regulators block or unwind anticompetitive acquisitions.
analysis.headline: The merger-restriction bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit mergers above $5 billion or that give a buyer more than a third of a market, and more than a quarter of a labor market as an employer. It would let the FTC and the Justice Department reject proposed deals outright — instead of having to win a lawsuit — and would authorize them to unwind big past mergers, including a mandatory review of every large merger completed since 2000. It would also require merger reviewers to weigh effects on workers, layoffs, and collective bargaining, and it would roughly triple the annual funding of the FTC and the Justice Department's antitrust division to $1 billion each.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, whose wages and bargaining rights would become a formal part of merger review, including a 25% cap on an employer's share of a labor market. Consumers in concentrated markets, where consolidation has been linked to higher prices and reduced choice. Small businesses, family farms, and minority-owned firms that sell to or buy from consolidated industries, and which would gain a formal veto channel through the Small Business Administration and Minority Business Development Agency. Communities harmed by past mergers, which could seek their reversal.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, consumers, small businesses, family farms

how_it_helps.text: Outright bans mergers valued above $5 billion, deals giving the buyer more than 33% of a market, and deals giving a buyer more than 25% of a labor market as an employer.

Lets the FTC and the Justice Department reject acquisitions by agency decision after a 120-day review, rather than having to persuade a federal court, and limits the parties to one challenge in federal district court under a deferential standard.

Authorizes regulators to retroactively unwind mergers that left a buyer with more than 50% of a market or otherwise harmed competition, and requires immediate review of every merger consummated since January 1, 2000 that would qualify as prohibited.

Requires merger review to consider harms to workers, including significant layoffs, harm to collective bargaining agreements, and labor conditions, and lets the National Labor Relations Board object to deals that would create monopsony power over labor.

Gives other agencies, state attorneys general, and the public a formal role: the FTC and DOJ must share filings with state attorneys general and relevant federal agencies, take public comment for 60 days, and reject a deal if certain agencies object on stated grounds.
Authorizes $1 billion per year each for the FTC and the DOJ Antitrust Division, roughly triple their recent budgets, funded in part by antitrust fines and penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their shareholders, who would face bright-line bans on major acquisitions, steep new filing requirements (with executives facing up to 5 years in prison and 5% of parent-company revenue in fines for false filings), and the risk of unwinding deals already completed. Private equity firms and investment funds over $10 billion in assets, which would be treated as dominant firms and could be rejected if the buyer or seller had paid significant fines or settlements in the prior decade. Investment banks and law firms that advise on big deals, which would face slower, longer reviews and less deal volume.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large acquirers, private equity, deal advisers

drawbacks.text: The bright-line thresholds do not distinguish deals that would raise prices from those that might genuinely create efficiencies; a company at 34% market share buying a small rival is banned even if the deal would lower costs, and the bill forbids courts from weighing procompetitive benefits against anticompetitive harms.

Unwinding consummated mergers, including a mandatory sweep of every prohibited merger back to 2000, would create years of uncertainty for companies that built their businesses through past acquisitions, and reversing decades-old deals could disrupt jobs and operations of the merged firms.

The bill strips Supreme Court review of its decisions and concentrates all challenges in a single district court and the D.C. Circuit, which raises separation-of-powers concerns that even sympathetic antitrust scholars would flag, and gives the two enforcement agencies sweeping discretion on the theory that courts have under-enforced the antitrust laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: labor-market concentration and consolidation in food, retail, and healthcare have been linked to lower wages and higher prices, and the bill would address both prospectively and retroactively. But the design is aggressive in ways that carry real risks of overreach — categorical bans regardless of efficiencies, mandated unwinding of 20-plus years of completed mergers, and removal of Supreme Court oversight. A more moderate bill might have achieved much of the prospective gain with far less disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it never reached the floor for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 16, 2022 by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with eight original cosponsors — seven Democrats and one independent — and was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

No Republican signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill would have banned mergers over $5 billion, deals giving a buyer more than a third of a market, and deals giving an employer more than a quarter of a labor market.
The bill also would have empowered the FTC and DOJ to retroactively unwind mergers meeting anticompetitive criteria, such as leaving a buyer with more than 50% of a relevant market.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies and investment funds that buy competitors. With the bill dead, the existing merger regime — where the government must usually win a lawsuit after a deal closes and past consolidations stand — remained intact, and completed mergers faced no risk of being unwound.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eight original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so the chamber's partisan split was never tested; all nine original sponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Large corporate acquirers, including big tech platforms, retail and grocery chains, and hospital systems
industries.note: Bright-line bans would bar deals over $5 billion or above a 33% market share regardless of claimed efficiencies, and regulators could unwind past mergers, including a mandatory review of prohibited mergers back to 2000. Their interest in freely acquiring rivals conflicts with cheaper prices and higher wages for the public.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and large investment funds
industries.note: Funds with over $10 billion in assets would be treated as dominant firms, deals would face longer waits and exhaustive disclosure, and a fund's past fines or settlements over $1 million could get a deal rejected outright. Fund strategies built on rolling up smaller companies would be directly curtailed.

industries.industry: Investment banks, corporate law firms, and antitrust advisors
industries.note: Big-deal volume would shrink under categorical bans and 120-day reviews, cutting the fees that drive the industry, though new filing, certification, and litigation requirements would create some compliance work. Their business depends on transactions proceeding.

industries.industry: Small businesses, family farms, and minority-owned firms
industries.note: The bill gives the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy and the Commerce Department's minority business agency standing to object to deals that would materially harm small or minority-owned businesses, and reduces market power of the large buyers these firms sell to.
